intro.html: Praise can be a quiet word of thanks or a stadium roaring your name. These ten words cover the range: formal praise (commend), loud public praise (acclaim, laud, extol), honors you can hold (accolade, tribute), deep lifelong respect (revere, venerate), lifting someone up (exalt) and praise that goes too far (adulation).

To praise: commend (formally), laud and extol (highly, enthusiastically), exalt (raise high). Praise you receive: acclaim (public applause), accolade (an award or honor), tribute (a gift or act of respect), adulation (too much admiration). Deep respect: revere, venerate.

words.ex: The principal {commended} the students who organized the food drive.
words.ctx: Instead of scolding the lifeguard for leaving her chair, the manager {commended} her: she had left it only to help a tired swimmer out of the deep end.
words.etym: From Latin commendare, “to entrust, to recommend”: com (thoroughly) + mandare (to entrust, to order).

mn.text: Kai mends the broken garden fence all by himself, and the principal hands him a certificate in front of the whole school. To praise someone formally like that is to {commend} him.

scene.alt: A principal hands a certificate to a proud boy who mended the garden fence.

words.ctx: The young violinist’s concert earned instant {acclaim}: the audience rose to its feet, and the next morning every newspaper in the city praised her.
words.etym: From Latin acclamare, “to shout at”: ad (to) + clamare (to shout).

mn.text: Rosa plays her last note, and the whole hall rises, clapping and calling out “Bravo!” That storm of public praise is {acclaim}.

scene.alt: A violinist bows on stage while the audience claps and cheers.

words.ex: Critics {lauded} the new bridge as a work of art.
words.ctx: Though the inventor had been mocked for years, the scientists who once doubted him now {lauded} his work, calling it the most important discovery of the decade.
words.etym: From Latin laudare, “to praise,” from laus, praise.

mn.text: Grandpa Gus reads Pip’s poem and praises it so loud the whole street can hear: “Best poem ever written!” To praise that highly is to {laud}.

scene.alt: A grandfather loudly praises his grandson’s poem while the boy blushes.

words.ex: Nana never stops {extolling} the virtues of a good night’s sleep.
words.ctx: In every speech, the coach {extolled} her team’s hard work, praising the players’ early-morning practices even more than their victories.
words.etym: From Latin extollere, “to lift up”: ex (out, up) + tollere (to raise).

mn.text: After the beach volleyball final, the team lifts Rosa onto their shoulders and sings her praises. To lift someone up with praise is to {extol} her.

scene.alt: Two teammates lift a cheering girl high onto their shoulders on the beach.

words.def: an award, honor or expression of praise
words.ex: The firefighter received the town’s highest {accolade} for bravery.
words.ctx: Winning the science fair was nice, but the {accolade} Maya treasured most was a handwritten note from the judge calling her experiment the cleverest she had ever seen.
words.etym: From French accolade, “an embrace around the neck,” once part of the ceremony of making a knight.

mn.text: The judge hangs a gold medal around Dev’s neck for his science project. Col means neck, and an {accolade} is an honor like that.

scene.alt: A boy stands on a podium with a gold medal around his neck while a woman claps.

words.def: an act, statement or gift that shows respect or admiration
words.ex: The concert was a {tribute} to the town’s beloved music teacher.
words.ctx: When the old lighthouse keeper retired, the villagers paid him {tribute}: they renamed the harbor road in his honor and painted his portrait on the post office wall.
words.etym: From Latin tributum, “a payment,” from tribuere, “to assign, to pay.”
words.note: Long ago, tribute also meant a payment that one ruler forced another to make.

mn.cue: TREE-bute: a TREE planted in her honor
mn.text: When Ms. Ada retires, her students plant an oak in the schoolyard with a sign: “For Ms. Ada, who taught us to wonder.” The tree is a {tribute} to her.

labels.text: TREE-bute: a tree in her honor

scene.alt: Students plant a young tree with a sign in honor of their retiring teacher, who beams.

words.def: to feel deep respect and admiration for
words.ex: The young players {revere} their coach, who once played for the national team.
words.ctx: Though the old doctor had retired long ago, the townspeople still {revered} her, for she had cared for three generations of their families and never turned anyone away.
words.etym: From Latin revereri: re (thoroughly) + vereri (to stand in awe of). This ver is not the ver (true) of verify.

mn.cue: re-VEER: every eye VEERS toward her
mn.text: When Coach Tia walks onto the field, every player’s eyes veer toward her with awe: she once played for the national team. They {revere} her.

labels.text: re-VEER: all eyes turn to her

scene.alt: Three young players gaze in admiration at their coach, a former national team player.

words.def: to regard with deep respect, often for age or wisdom
words.ex: The villagers {venerate} the ancient oak that has shaded their square for five hundred years.
words.ctx: The young chefs {venerated} Granny Mae: at ninety, she had cooked in the same kitchen for seventy years, and half the recipes in the town’s cookbook began with hers.
words.etym: From Latin venerari, “to honor, to adore.”

mn.cue: ven-ERA-te: honored from an old ERA
mn.text: Every spring the town gathers under the five-hundred-year-old oak, a survivor from a long-ago era, and leaves flowers at its roots. The townspeople {venerate} it.

scene.alt: People bow and bring flowers to an ancient oak tree.

words.def: to raise high in rank, power or praise
words.ex: The old legends {exalt} the village baker who fed everyone through the long winter.
words.ctx: Rather than take credit herself, the director {exalted} the quiet helpers in her speech, calling the stagehands the true stars of the show.
words.etym: From Latin exaltare, “to raise high”: ex (up) + altus (high), as in altitude.
words.note: Exalt (to raise up, to praise) is not exult (to rejoice): you exalt a hero; you exult in a victory.

mn.text: The village lifts its brave baker onto the tallest platform in the square, as high as the rooftops. To raise someone high in honor is to {exalt} her.

scene.alt: A baker in a sash stands high on a platform while villagers cheer below.

words.ex: The young singer was overwhelmed by the {adulation} of her fans.
words.ctx: After his famous goal, the striker basked in the {adulation} of the crowd, though his coach reminded him that the cheering would fade if he stopped practicing.
words.etym: From Latin adulari, “to fawn upon,” a word first used of dogs wagging their tails at their masters.

mn.text: The fans scream, wave signs and toss flowers, adding praise upon praise until the young singer can barely be seen. That flood of admiration is {adulation}.

scene.alt: Screaming fans toss flowers and wave signs at a startled young singer.

part of speech
the kind of praise
after.cap: Who is praising, and how much?

after.html: exalt (raise up, praise) and exult (rejoice) differ by one letter. The fans exult in the win; the poem exalts the hero. And adulation goes beyond admiration: it is praise piled so high that it starts to feel like flattery.

items.q: Which sentence uses the right word?
choices: The poem exalts the courage of the firefighters.
The fans exalted when their team won.
She exalted over her perfect test score.
items.why: Exalt means to praise or raise up (exalt the firefighters). To rejoice is to exult: the fans exulted.

items.q: Which word suggests praise that goes too far?
items.why: Adulation is excessive admiration, bordering on flattery or hero worship.

items.q: True or false: an accolade is a kind of honor or award.
items.why: True. An accolade is an award or expression of praise, like a medal or a glowing review.

items.q: Which pair are closest in meaning?
items.why: Revere and venerate both mean to feel deep, lasting respect for someone or something.
